overview:
Ireland is a green island on the western edge of Europe, facing the Atlantic Ocean, with Great Britain across the Irish Sea to the east. The Republic of Ireland covers about five-sixths of the island, roughly the size of West Virginia; the northeastern corner, Northern Ireland, is part of the United Kingdom. The capital, Dublin, sits on the east coast at the mouth of the River Liffey, a city of Georgian brick houses, old pubs, and a university library holding a 1,200-year-old illustrated Bible, the Book of Kells.

About 5.3 million people live in the Republic. English is spoken by everyone, and Irish, a Celtic language, is the first official language, taught in every school and spoken daily in some western areas called the Gaeltacht. Ireland is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union. Once one of Europe's poorer countries, from which millions emigrated, it is now one of the richest, home to the European headquarters of many technology companies. Irish music, literature, and the celebration of St. Patrick's Day have spread around the world.
landAndNature: Ireland is shaped like a saucer: a central lowland of bogs, lakes, and pastures ringed by coastal hills and mountains. The highest peak, Carrauntoohil in County Kerry, reaches 1,038 meters. Mild, wet Atlantic weather keeps the grass so green that the island is called the Emerald Isle, and it almost never gets very hot or very cold. The west coast is wild and rugged: the Cliffs of Moher drop 214 meters into the ocean, and the Burren is a strange gray limestone landscape where Arctic and Mediterranean flowers grow side by side. The Giant's Causeway, in Northern Ireland, is famous for its hexagonal basalt columns. The River Shannon is the longest in the British Isles. Red deer roam Killarney, seals bask on rocks, and puffins nest on the Skellig islands.
peopleAndCulture: The Irish are famous for talk, music, and storytelling. Traditional sessions in pubs bring together fiddles, tin whistles, bodhrán drums, and uilleann pipes, and Irish dancing, with its fast footwork and still arms, is performed worldwide. Ireland has produced four Nobel Prize winners in literature, including W. B. Yeats and Samuel Beckett, along with James Joyce and Oscar Wilde. Gaelic games are unique to Ireland: hurling, played with wooden sticks and a small ball, is one of the fastest field sports on Earth, and Gaelic football fills stadiums every summer. Rugby and soccer are also loved. Foods include soda bread, Irish stew, and potatoes in many forms, and St. Patrick's Day on March 17 brings parades in every town.
history: Farmers built the great stone tomb of Newgrange around 3200 BC, older than the pyramids. Celtic culture arrived later, and in the 400s St. Patrick spread Christianity; Irish monks then produced beautiful manuscripts and carried learning across Europe during the Dark Ages. Vikings founded Dublin around 841, and Norman knights arrived in 1169, beginning 750 years of English involvement. English and Scottish settlers took land in the 1600s, and Catholics lost most of their rights. The Great Famine of 1845 to 1852, when the potato crop failed, killed about a million people and forced another million to emigrate. An uprising in 1916 and a war of independence led to the Irish Free State in 1922, with the north remaining British. Ireland became a republic in 1949 and joined the European Union in 1973.
funFacts: Halloween grew out of the ancient Irish festival of Samhain, when people believed spirits walked among the living.
Ireland has no native snakes, which legend credits to St. Patrick but scientists credit to the Ice Age and the surrounding sea.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol, and Ireland is the only country with a musical instrument as its official emblem.
About 70 million people around the world claim Irish ancestry, more than 13 times the population of Ireland itself.
Newgrange, a stone tomb built about 5,200 years ago, is lit by the rising sun only at the winter solstice.
